events.text: The Elders' Council meets without you, which it has not done in years. In the morning the eldest of them brings you their answer on a sheet of red paper: the match you arranged will shame the ancestors, and not one of them will light the incense at that wedding.

choices.text: Overrule them before the ancestral tablets
Sit with them night after night until they come round (it may not work)
Bow to the Council and break the match off

events.text: The tablets of the ancestors have been turned to face the wall. Nobody admits to doing it, and nobody turns them back. The Elders' Council lets the whole house know why: the match you made for a child of the house is one the founders would never have made.

choices.text: Turn the tablets back yourself and hold the wedding anyway
Bring the old records and argue the match is no stranger than the founders' own (it may not work)
Let the tablets win, and send gifts to end the match

events.text: The cousins of the branch lines have been eating together a great deal this spring, always at the far end of the lands, never inviting you. Tonight a kitchen servant comes to your door shaking: at the next rite, they mean to name one of their own head of the house.

choices.text: Move first, before they can gather (it may fail)
Invite them to the council table, with a field and silver from the treasury
Do nothing; cousins talk, that is all

events.text: A copy of the seal of the house is found in a cadet branch's storeroom, carved very well. The branch lines say it was made in case the old one was ever lost. Their stewards have already been seen measuring the ancestral hall.

choices.text: Seize the copy and the ones who carved it (it may fail)
Give the branch lines a share of the lands and a voice in the house
Laugh it off; a seal is only wood

events.text: The rents came in well this year, and the treasury is lighter than last year anyway. The chief steward has an answer for every question, and the answers are all a little too smooth.

choices.text: Sit down with the ledgers yourself, every page (it may fail)
Dismiss the chief steward and appoint another
Let it go; every house loses a little to its stewards

events.text: A tenant farmer walks two days to the ancestral hall to ask, very politely, why the granary of the house is selling rice in the market town at half the price. You did not know the granary was selling rice at all.

choices.text: Ride to the granary and count the sacks yourself (it may fail)
Turn the stewards of that granary out of the house
Thank the farmer and send them home with a gift

events.text: Your eldest and your most gifted child are no longer speaking. The Elders back the eldest, by custom; the stewards back the gifted one, for the good of the house; and the cousins of the branch lines watch the two of them the way crows watch a field.

choices.text: Name the eldest, as custom asks
Name the ablest, whatever custom says
Name nobody yet, and give each side something to keep the peace

events.text: In the training courtyard your two eldest children draw real swords on each other in front of the whole house. Servants pull them apart before blood is spilled, and the question nobody has dared to ask is asked at last: which of them will hold the seat after you?

choices.text: The eldest, by custom; let the house hear it today
The stronger of the two; let the house hear that too
Neither, yet; each gets a field and a warning
